text:
“I remember,” he began, “a day in the month of March, when you came to see me at my house for the first time. I was asleep. You were almost a child then, or seemed to be, and you showed me a gold bracelet. Yes!… and now I no longer have that house, or at least I must leave it, because there has been a scandal and people avoid greeting me… Do you know? It means that you will have a house, and one more beautiful and richer than mine, since Rafa spends willingly. Provided, however, that you do not grow too fat… Rafa, I warn you, abhors women who are too fat. Then I also remember an excursion we took together, on the shores of a certain lake… But it was for one night only; perhaps you have lost all memory of it amid so many things.”

He looked at her, questioned her, intimidated her with his sinister eyes.

“Tell me a little about your life, then!… Have you no voice left?”

His sister asked in a firm, simple tone:

“Why have you come?”

He stared at her for a moment, his eyes gleaming brightly:

“I was passing by,” he answered; “the wall is not high; I felt like paying you a visit.”

“Why have you come?” she repeated again, in a deeper voice.

“Ah!… Perhaps you thought you would never see me again? Had you already put your heart at rest?”

A wicked, gloomy anger showed fleetingly in her, as it did in her brother’s face.

“I have done you no harm,” she said sharply, with complete certainty.

“You?”

“No harm,” she insisted, even more sharply.

He sprang to his feet, livid, as though to seize her.

“No, do not touch me!” she commanded, shielding herself with both arms. “If you wanted me, I was yours; you could freely have done with me whatever you pleased… Do not forget that!”

“What are you saying?” he murmured, surprised by these words, struck full on by this truth.

“When I was, as you said, a child, when I came to your house for the first time, and afterward, and always, until the day you fled, you could have done with me whatever you pleased. I would never have taken revenge or complained.”

She too paused, since he was silent, struck with astonishment.

“But what are you asking of me now?” Loretta added.

“What am I asking you?… A little clarification, a trifling thing: for what reason did you become Rafa’s mistress?”

She turned her eyes irresolutely elsewhere, toward the motionless trees, toward the trembling stars, toward the luminous shadow of the cerulean night.

“Answer!”

“I do not know.”

“For love?”

“No.”

“For money?”

“Not that either.”

“Did he perhaps take you by force?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“I do not know, I do not know!…” she said nervously. “Why do you want to torment me?”

“Answer: did you love him? Do you love him?”

“No. I said no.”

She sensed that she was saving herself with these words, and repeated once more:

“Neither before nor now; I do not love him.”

And moreover, it was indeed true.

A kind of vertigo passed through the eyes of the man staring at her; a sign, almost already a smile, almost a kiss, creased his bitter mouth.

“Then why did you do this?”

“I myself could not tell you,” his sister confessed. “It was madness, a moment of thoughtlessness, something unforeseen and easy, without seriousness yet almost necessary… One day I did this, and I cannot even tell you the reason. Perhaps because you had tormented me so much, perhaps because I made the mistake of climbing a staircase… I do not know, I do not know!”

And now she was no longer afraid of him; she spoke to him almost gently, her lovely color returning to her blooming cheeks, passing a ringed hand over her white temple and smoothing her hair with one of her habitual gestures.

“And I?” her brother murmured after being silent.

“You?”

“Yes, Lora, I, who loved you with such anguish, I, who fled desperately so as not to hurt you?…”

She hesitated a little, then said:

“You did not want me… you did not want me even when I wept over it, therefore…”

In the terrible simplicity of these words she gathered all the logic of her little woman’s heart, solved her little feminine enigma, in which the maddest love had ultimately been nothing but a murky curiosity. She could go no further; the whole story of her great sin ended in this little reflection: “You did not want me, therefore…”

And he lowered his face, then began rapping his knuckles on the little wicker table, which rocked.

“Therefore,” he said, with bitterness and mockery, “you simply needed someone to lay you down hard, with your shoulders upon a pillow, someone to make you finally utter that little cry… Who that person was mattered little. I had tormented you greatly… did you say tormented?… Very well, so be it! But in any case you chose yourself a rich man, to sweeten the pains of martyrdom; in exchange you wanted a few dresses, a few jewels, a house that will end by becoming yours… there, and you have all this!”

“I wanted,” she explained, “to choose for myself a life different from the one I was leading: nothing else. Perhaps I was also mistaken.”

He stared at her again with a doubtful look, then changed his mind:

“Why are you alone this evening?”

“I am alone many times,” she answered.

They fell silent; a long silence held sway over their uneasiness. He waited for her to speak; she was waiting for his words. And they scrutinized one another attentively; each sought to read the other’s heart.

“Then,” he resumed after that pause, “then you have nothing to tell me?”

“Yes, many things… but I am afraid of you.”

“And you are right,” her brother said. “I have reached that hour when nothing and no one is respected any longer, when an entire history goes to meet its final peril. Yet I am listening, if you have something to tell me, and I am still listening kindly, Lora, because I am still the same… I repeat: still the same.”

And in these last words he put into his voice an accent as gentle as a caress.

“Sit down,” he added; “come closer to me.”

“No!” she said twice, “no.”

“Are you afraid?”

She did not answer; but it seemed that an anguish, a pity, a compassion almost bordering on revulsion, was choking her soul in that refusal.

On the threshold of the half-dark room, Lazzara’s figure appeared, full of hesitation, yet with the air of being there to bring her help.

The man turned toward her with a sudden movement:

“What do you want?” he assailed her.

The girl did not answer; her frightened eyes moved from one to the other, as though trying to guess.

But Loretta said to her:

“Do not be afraid, Lazzara. Go up to your room and sleep. My brother will leave shortly.”

“Your brother, madam?…” the girl uttered, unable to believe herself for amazement.

“Go up and sleep, Lazzara,” Lora commanded briefly.

She withdrew in small steps, saying nothing, and disappeared into the darkness. Shortly afterward, from within the thickness of the ancient wall there burst forth the sound of running water, which in the resonance of the night filled the deep house with sound. Then it ceased: the lofty rooms fell asleep.
